name: Times club monthly special crossword No 20,175

solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Agree with sister in trivial chat, about to erode limestone below?

indicators.note: the agreeing word and the sister sit inside the chat word
about means turned round, so the whole built string is read from the end

blocks.note: yak is idle chatter
to fit is to agree or match
SR is the abbreviation for sister

explanation.surface: Someone agrees with their sister over idle gossip, then sets off to wear away the rock underfoot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like part of 'about to erode' but signals reading the built string backwards. Karst is limestone country riddled by water dissolving it underground, hence the question-marked 'below'.
explanation.definitionFit: To karstify is to turn terrain into karst, the cave-pocked landscape made when water dissolves limestone beneath the surface.

clue.text: Where rising leak loses energy, try universal plugs, waterproof

indicators.note: in a down clue rising means read from bottom to top
loses means a letter is taken away
a plug sits inside a hole, so these letters go inside

blocks.note: taken as written, then turned round
E is the symbol for energy, the letter lost
to have a go is to try
U is the film rating for universal

explanation.surface: Where water is getting in, try a universal plug to make it watertight.
explanation.walkthrough: KAEL loses its E to give KAL, and GO and U go inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A kagoul is a lightweight hooded rain jacket, a waterproof garment.

clue.text: Victorian con man, a troublesome young person putting the other half first

indicators.note: moving the back half to the front rotates the word round its midpoint

blocks.note: a little terror is a badly behaved child

explanation.surface: A nineteenth-century swindler is described as a nuisance youngster with things back to front.
explanation.walkthrough: Victorian means from the Australian state of Victoria, not the era: rort is Australian slang for a scam.
explanation.definitionFit: Rorter is Australian slang for a swindler who works a rort, a fraudulent scheme.

clue.text: Cap on India's prime cultivated land united one of its states

indicators.note: prime means first, so only the opening letter is taken
cultivated land is turned over, so these letters are turned into a new order

blocks.note: a tam is a Scottish woollen cap
the first letter of India
the letters of land rearranged
U is the abbreviation for united

explanation.surface: Topping India's best farmland unified one of its regions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Its' refers back to India, so the definition depends on the wordplay's own word.
explanation.definitionFit: Tamil Nadu is a state in the far south of India, with Chennai as its capital.

clue.text: Identify as suspect batter where food can be picked up

definitions.text: where food can be picked up

blocks.note: to finger someone is to point them out to police
to buffet is to strike repeatedly

explanation.surface: A witness picks out the person who beat someone up, in a crime story.
explanation.walkthrough: Batter tempts as cooking mixture next to food, but here it is the verb to strike.
explanation.definitionFit: A finger buffet is a meal of small items eaten with the hands rather than cutlery.

clue.text: Wandering hiker's drinking bag, primarily one made of skin

indicators.note: a wandering hiker strays from the set path, so the letters stray from their order
primarily points to the opening letter of the word before it
something drinking takes another thing into itself

blocks.note: the word hiker, its possessive ending dropped, is the anagram fodder
the first letter of bag

explanation.surface: A trekker carries a drinking bag, a traditional one made of animal skin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drinking bag' looks like the definition but splits: drinking is the container signal and bag supplies its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A kirbeh is an Arabic leather water bottle, a container sewn from hide.

clue.text: Coroner's investigation misses parts surrounding the heart, previously branded?

indicators.note: missing means going without, here the two letters flanking the middle one

blocks.note: a coroner holds an inquest into a death

explanation.surface: A coroner's inquiry overlooks the organs around a heart that had once been marked.
explanation.walkthrough: INQUEST has U at its centre; the Q and E either side of it are dropped.
explanation.definitionFit: Inust is an obsolete word for burnt in, as a brand is burnt into skin, hence 'previously'.

clue.text: Powdery deposit from work unit, unexceptional in British Library

indicators.note: one thing set in another sits inside it

blocks.note: the erg is a unit of work in physics
meh is slang for so-so
BL is the abbreviation for British Library

explanation.surface: Dust settles from a mediocre department in a great London library.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is German for mountain flour; meh is a modern slang shrug meaning so-so.
explanation.definitionFit: Bergmehl is a fine earthy powder of diatom shells, a deposit sometimes called mountain meal.

clue.text: Arkansas doctor's vague about Spenser's rash behaviour

indicators.note: about means around, so the vague word wraps the others

blocks.note: AR is the US postal code for Arkansas
DR is the abbreviation for doctor; the 's is a joining is
hazy means unclear

explanation.surface: A physician from Arkansas is unclear on the poet Spenser's reckless conduct.
explanation.walkthrough: Spenser's flags an obsolete word used by the Elizabethan poet; the doctor's 's is read as 'is', joining the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Hazardry, from hazard, meant dicing or reckless risk-taking in Spenser's English.

clue.text: Interrupting ramble, continue to stuff face

indicators.note: something interrupting breaks into the middle of another thing
to here means attached after, so one piece follows the other

blocks.note: to ram is to stuff or cram
on as in carry on, keep going
to gad is to wander about

explanation.surface: Someone breaks off a rambling story to carry on stuffing their face with food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Face' is not the mouth being stuffed but a typeface; the inserted pair sits after the first two letters of the outer word.
explanation.definitionFit: Garamond is a classic serif typeface, and printers call any type design a face.

clue.text: Hard stuff requiring skill to take one's place in knowledge test

indicators.note: taking a place means one thing stands where another stood, swapping it out

blocks.note: a quiz tests what you know
art as in craft or knack
I is the Roman numeral one, the letter swapped out

explanation.surface: A tough question in a quiz needs skill to answer.
explanation.walkthrough: ART replaces the I of QUIZ. 'Hard stuff' hints at strong drink but means a hard mineral.
explanation.definitionFit: Quartz is a very hard crystalline mineral, rating seven on the Mohs scale.

clue.text: Millions desperately unwell graze cattle food

indicators.note: something done desperately is frantic and disordered, so the letters fall out of order

blocks.note: M is the abbreviation for millions
the letters of these two words rearranged

explanation.surface: Huge numbers of sick animals are grazing on fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The mangel-wurzel is a large beet grown as winter fodder for livestock.

clue.text: Dubious value of colourful part for viewers

indicators.note: something dubious is not straight, so the letters are not in their proper order

blocks.note: taken as written, the anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Questioning whether a vividly coloured section is worth it for the audience.
explanation.walkthrough: The viewers are eyes, not an audience: the uvea is the pigmented layer of the eye, including the iris.
explanation.definitionFit: Uveal is the adjective for the uvea, the eye's pigmented middle layer that gives the iris its colour.

clue.text: Most of distant traffic wheels showing rubber-like substance

indicators.note: most of a word means all but its final letter
wheels as a verb means turns round and about, so the letters spin into a new order

blocks.note: remote means far away
traffic as trade, selling

explanation.surface: Far-off cars on the road reveal some rubbery stuff, perhaps their tyres.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Traffic wheels' reads as cars, but traffic is a noun for trading and wheels is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: An elastomer is a polymer with rubber's elasticity, stretching and returning to shape.

clue.text: The writer is Marsh, to criticise the female poet

blocks.note: the setter as 'the writer' is I, so 'the writer is' becomes I am
a bog is a marsh
to rap is to rebuke
the female pronoun

explanation.surface: The author declares they are Marsh and sets about attacking a woman poet.
explanation.walkthrough: Marsh looks like a surname, perhaps the novelist Ngaio Marsh, but it is a common noun.
explanation.definitionFit: An iambographer is a writer of iambic verse, especially the satirical iambi of ancient Greece.

clue.text: Outstanding special constable enclosed youth initially going bad

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the first letter is used

blocks.note: ace means excellent
SC is the abbreviation for special constable
enc is the abbreviation for enclosed, as on a letter
the first letter of youth

explanation.surface: A first-rate part-time police officer locked up a young person who was turning to crime.
explanation.walkthrough: Enclosed looks like a container signal but gives its letter-writing abbreviation. A special constable is a British volunteer police officer.
explanation.definitionFit: Acescency is the state of turning sour, as wine or milk begins to spoil.

clue.text: A television in a cabinet also containing one sounding board

indicators.note: one thing in another goes inside it
containing means holding within, here a second item

blocks.note: taken as written
TV is the abbreviation for television
taken as written, at the front
a box is a cabinet or case
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A TV set in a cabinet also holding one board for sound.
explanation.walkthrough: The cabinet holds two things at different points: the television pair just after its first letter and the one just before its last.
explanation.definitionFit: An abat-voix is a canopy over a pulpit that reflects the preacher's voice towards the congregation.

clue.text: Objection about concessionary gesture working, having teeth, with knobs on!

indicators.note: about means around, so the objection goes round the rest

blocks.note: a but is an objection, as in no buts
a nod concedes a point
on as in switched on, operating

explanation.surface: A complaint about a reluctant nod given at work, with knobs on, as the playground retort goes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With knobs on' is a British retort meaning 'and the same to you', but here it describes knobbly teeth.
explanation.definitionFit: Bunodont describes molars with rounded cusps, like those of pigs and humans.

clue.text: Empty threat is routine in paperwork by usual unoccupied workers

indicators.note: one thing set in another goes inside it
unoccupied means emptied of its contents, leaving just the outer letters

blocks.note: bumf is British slang for tedious paperwork
a rut is a dull routine
the outer letters of usual
men as in workers or hands

explanation.surface: Bureaucratic paperwork from idle staff is just a hollow threat.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is a Latin phrase; 'paperwork' is British slang that solvers abroad may not know, meaning tedious official documents.
explanation.definitionFit: Brutum fulmen is Latin for a senseless thunderbolt, used for a menace that has no force behind it.

clue.text: Good writer's need to match tree

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for good
a pen needs ink to write
to go with is to match

explanation.surface: A decent author needs to find a matching tree, perhaps for paper.
explanation.definitionFit: The ginkgo, or maidenhair tree, is an ancient Chinese species with fan-shaped leaves.

clue.text: Trail with half-turn to the north where giants supposedly live

indicators.note: half means only part of the word is kept, its second half lost
in a down clue going to the north means read upwards

blocks.note: to drag is to trail behind
taken as written, then halved

explanation.surface: A walking trail with a sharp turn northwards leads to the land of giants.
explanation.walkthrough: TU is half of TURN; DRAG plus TU is then read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: In Norse myth Utgard is the outer realm of the giants, beyond the world of men.

clue.text: Somewhat disastrous sea upended old packet

indicators.note: somewhat means only part of what follows, a stretch inside the words

blocks.note: the letters run across the three words, from the end of the first to the start of the last

explanation.surface: A dreadful sea capsized something, perhaps a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upended' seems to signal a reversal, but the answer reads forwards inside the words.
explanation.definitionFit: Trousseau once meant a small bundle or package, before it came to mean a bride's outfit of clothes and linen.

clue.text: Holy man had us converted

indicators.note: converted means changed into another form, so the letters change order

blocks.note: taken as written, the anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A religious man won us over to his faith.
explanation.definitionFit: A sadhu is a Hindu ascetic who has renounced worldly life.

clue.text: Cape to raise for sharp drop

blocks.note: C is the map abbreviation for cape
to lift is to raise

explanation.surface: Climbers head up a headland to reach a steep fall.
explanation.definitionFit: Clift is an old variant of cliff, a sheer rock face where the ground falls away.

clue.text: Imitation gold rings are on either side of badger's head

indicators.note: things on either side of another flank it, one before and one after
the head is the very front, so only the opening letter is flanked, not the whole word

blocks.note: two rings, each round like the letter O
to ride someone is to badger them; its head is the first letter

explanation.surface: Fake gold bands are placed around a badger's head, a mock trophy.
explanation.walkthrough: The rings flank only the head of RIDE, its R, giving O, R, O and then the rest of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Oroide is a brassy alloy of copper and zinc or tin made to look like gold in cheap jewellery.

clue.text: Academic grasping unknown fringes of Greek almost possesses understanding of Himalayan language

indicators.note: grasping means holding something within
the fringes of a word are its edges, its outer letters
almost means not quite all, so the last letter is dropped

blocks.note: a don is a university teacher
algebra uses x, y and z for unknowns
the outer letters of Greek
has means possesses

explanation.surface: A scholar who has a partial grasp of Greek also understands a mountain tongue.
explanation.walkthrough: The unknown sits just after the academic's first letter, a common place for an inserted letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Dzongkha is the national language of Bhutan, a kingdom in the eastern Himalayas.

clue.text: Ionian ancestor ready for Vietnamese like this

blocks.note: ready is slang for cash, and the xu is a small Vietnamese coin
thus means in this way

explanation.surface: A forebear from Ionia sets out a model to follow for the Vietnamese.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ready' means prepared on the surface but is British slang for money, as in 'the ready'.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Xuthus was the father of Ion, from whom the Ionian Greeks took their name.

clue.text: Lifeless year before depression stops in a habit?

indicators.note: to stop something is to plug it, sitting inside it

blocks.note: Y is the abbreviation for year
a col is a dip between peaks
someone in a habit is clad, dressed

explanation.surface: A nun in her habit falls dead after a year of depression.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Depression' suggests low spirits but is a mountain dip, and 'in a habit' means dressed.
explanation.definitionFit: Clay-cold describes a corpse, as cold as earth, so without life.
